main.t: The bone of the lower side of the skull, around the ear (temporal bone).

simpler.t: The temporal bone is the skull bone around your ear.

deeper.t: Its petrous part houses the middle and inner ear.

facts.t: It forms the lower side of the skull, below the parietal bone.
It is paired: one on each side of the brain case.
Its zygomatic process reaches forwards to form the back of the zygomatic arch.

simpler.t: It is at the side of your head, around and behind your ear.

deeper.t: Inside the skull, its petrous ridge separates the middle and posterior cranial fossae.

items.name: Zygomatic process
items.t: Projects forwards to form the back of the zygomatic arch.

items.name: Mastoid process
items.t: A large bump behind the earlobe, where muscles attach.

items.name: Petrous part
items.t: A dense diagonal ridge inside the skull, holding the middle and inner ear.

items.name: External and internal acoustic meatuses
items.t: The ear canal outside; inside, an opening for nerves of hearing, balance and the face.

items.name: Mandibular fossa and articular tubercle
items.t: A hollow and a ridge in front of the ear canal, for the jaw joint.

items.name: Styloid process
items.t: A pen-like spike pointing down, for small muscles and a ligament to the hyoid.

items.name: Stylomastoid foramen and carotid canal
items.t: Openings for the nerve to the face muscles, and a major artery to the brain.

simpler.t: It has a flat upper part, a bump behind the ear and a dense ridge that holds the ear.

deeper.t: Its name may come from the temple, where hair often turns grey first, marking the passage of time.

facts.t: Its dense petrous part encloses the small bones and canals of hearing and balance.
In front of the ear canal, the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle make the skull’s half of the jaw joint.
The zygomatic process joins the zygomatic bone, forming the arch from which a chewing muscle arises.

simpler.t: It holds your ear, makes the socket for your jaw and anchors a chewing muscle.

items.name: Temporomandibular joint
items.t: The condyle of the mandible meets its mandibular fossa and articular tubercle.

items.name: Zygomatic bone
items.t: Its temporal process joins the zygomatic process to form the zygomatic arch.

items.name: Facial nerve
items.t: Controls the muscles of facial expression; it leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen.

items.name: Vestibulocochlear nerve
items.t: Carries hearing and balance from the inner ear, through the internal acoustic meatus.

items.name: Internal carotid artery
items.t: Passes through its carotid canal to reach the brain.

items.name: Auditory ossicles
items.t: The three tiny bones of the middle ear, inside its petrous part.

simpler.t: It holds the ear and the jaw joint, and important nerves and an artery pass through it.

facts.t: Its flat squamous part, on the side of the brain case, forms from membrane; its base parts form from cartilage.
The mastoid process enlarges during early childhood.
The mastoid process is larger in males.
facts.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20). Gray’s 1918 (7.2) says it is larger in the male (supporting only).

items.injury: A blow that fractures the base of the skull (basilar fracture).
items.damaged: The internal carotid artery, in the carotid canal of the temporal bone.
items.cannotDo: Rely on a normal blood supply to the brain on that side.
items.why: The internal carotid is one of the two main arteries supplying the brain.

items.injury: Swelling or injury of the facial nerve as it leaves the stylomastoid foramen (as in Bell’s palsy).
items.cannotDo: Close the eye, smile or raise the eyebrow on that side.
items.why: The facial nerve controls the muscles of facial expression.
items.check: Bell’s palsy and nerve injury at the foramen are not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20); the nerve’s course and role are.

items.q: Explain how the temporal bone takes part in the jaw joint.
model: The mandibular fossa is a deep oval hollow in front of the ear canal.
The articular tubercle is a smooth ridge just in front of it.
The condyle of the mandible sits in the fossa when the mouth is closed.
As the mouth opens, it glides forwards onto the tubercle.

items.q: Compare the external and internal acoustic meatuses.
model: External: the ear canal, a large opening on the side of the skull.
Sound travels in it to the eardrum.
Internal: an opening inside the skull, on the petrous ridge.
It carries the nerves of hearing, balance and the face.

items.q: Predict what you can feel just behind your earlobe, and what it is for.
model: A large bump on the mastoid part of the temporal bone.

check.stem: Which nerve leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen?
check.why: The nerve to the muscles of facial expression, the facial nerve, exits here.

check.stem: Which part of the temporal bone houses the middle and inner ear?
check.why: Small cavities inside the petrous ridge house the middle and inner ears.

check.stem: Which artery passes through the carotid canal?
check.why: The internal carotid artery continues through the carotid canal to the brain.
